senses: An adjustable loop of rope, such as the one placed around the neck in hangings, or the one at the end of a lasso.
ety: From Middle English nose (“noose, loop”), of unclear origin. Possibly from Old French nos or Old Occitan nous, nos, nominative singular or accusative plural of nou (“knot”), with a required change in meaning shifting from the "knot" itself to the "loop" created by the knot. If so, then cognate with French nœud (“knot”), Portuguese nó (“knot”) and Spanish nudo (“knot”). Compare node and knot. Alternatively, and perhaps more likely, borrowed from Middle Low German nȫse (“loop, noose, snare”), itself of obscure origin. senses: A pyriform object.
ety: Borrowing from New Latin pyrifōrmis, from pyrum (“a pear”) + -fōrmis (“-form, -shaped”, adjectival suffix). Doublet of pyriformis.

senses: Gram flour, as used in Indian and Burmese cuisine.
A fruit-bearing tree, Ziziphus jujuba or Ziziphus zizyphus.
The fruit of this tree.
A fruit-bearing tree, Ziziphus mauritiana.
The fruit of this tree.
ety: From Middle English jujube, from Medieval Latin jujuba or Old French jujube, perhaps via Old Occitan from Classical Latin zīzyphum, zīzyphus, from Ancient Greek ζίζυφον (zízuphon)․ First attested in the 14th century.

senses: An exceptor.
ety: Borrowed from Latin excipiēns, present participle of excipiō. See except.

senses: A man who operates, manages, and maintains an engine.
A locomotive engineer; (sometimes) any footplateman.
A navy sailor who operates, manages, and maintains engines and various other shipboard equipment (such as one with the United States Navy EN occupational rating).
examples: At one corner of the room three enginemen were lost in serious discussion; in other corners, mécaniciens and chauffeurs were quietly talking, playing draughts, reading or eating.

senses: An edible leafy vegetable, Beta vulgaris subsp. cicla, with a slightly bitter taste.
Artichoke leaves and shoots, blanched to eat.
ety: From earlier card (remodelled after chardoon, obsolete form of cardoon), from Middle French carde, from Latin carduus (“thistle”). Doublet of cardoon.

senses: A collection of hymns; a hymn book.
ety: From Middle English hymnale, from Medieval Latin hymnāle, noun use of neuter of hymnālis.

senses: Extravagantly showy; shiny, glittery.
examples: Kanye, who had a blingy neck chain with Jesus icon - a Jesus Christ with aquatic blue, diamond eyes - tried, unsuccessfully, to get the jeweller to turn Christ's eyes darker and the whole icon a shade darker than it was.
Adam Perry Lang is at the opposite end of the grilling spectrum, a blingy S.U.V. to Mallmann’s muddy old Land Rover.

senses: A tarpaulin or plastic waterproof sheet.
A grouch or killjoy.
ety: Named after the main character in a children's book by Dr. Seuss, How the Grinch Stole Christmas! (1957). Coined as early as 1953, the term was initially used for a fictitious bird named the "Beagle-Beaked-Bald-Headed Grinch" in Scrambled Eggs Super!; it became associated with the character in a poem published in the May 1955 issue of Redbook, "The Hoobub and the Grinch". Likely a corruption of grouch.

senses: A hot, dry wind that blows across the Persian Gulf during the summer
A white, albuminous, fibrous substance, formed in the coagulation of the blood.
An albuminous body, resembling animal fibrin in composition, found in cereal grains and similar seeds; vegetable fibrin.
ety: From fibre + -in (used to form chemical names of proteins, etc).

senses: One who tries to eat only locally grown foods.
ety: From loca(l) + -vore. Coined by Jen Maiser, Jessica Prentice, Sage Van Wing, and DeDe Sampson, co-founders of the “Locavores” web site in 2005.
examples: They are a locavore’s (someone who eats food produced within 100 miles of he lives) paradise.

senses: Within the cavity of the peritoneum.
A syllable that can be either short or long.
An Argand lamp.
Able or intending to provide salvation or redemption.
ety: From Late Latin salvificus, from Latin salvus (“saved, safe”) + facio (“make”).

senses: A manufactured regenerated cellulosic fiber.
ety: Name chosen by the National Retail Dry Goods Association of America, probably from French rayon (“a beam of light, ray”) and so called because it is shiny; however, the Oxford English Dictionary states that it is apparently a blend of ray + cotton.

senses: A headcloth worn by pharaohs.
To daub or cover with gum.
Someone who acts in a clownlike manner.
To settle a jointure upon.
ety: Inherited from Middle English joynture, from Old French jointure, from Latin iūnctūra. Doublet of juncture.

senses: One who has, or attempts to acquire, a monopoly on something.
Prone to licking.
examples: He was a proper dog; a great, woolly, lolloping beast with huge paddy paws, a waggy tail and a very licky tongue.
As soon as the dog was safely enclosed within the area of our legs, it became happy and licky. He ran to one then the other. Then he sat on the floor and watched us watching him.

senses: One who, or that which, dissolves or dissipates.
examples: Thou kind dissolver of encroaching care.

senses: A sort of Russian isinglass, made from the air bladder of the sturgeon. Among its uses is clarifying wine, restoration, and making gelatin.
ety: From French carlock, from Russian карлу́к (karlúk).

senses: to cut again.
examples: The footage of the first Christopher Street demonstration parade came from Lilli Vencenz. She made a film called Gay and Proud and sent me a release on her footage so that I could recut it for GAY USA.

senses: A man who lives on or around the moors.
An automobile construction technique in which the body is integrated into a single unit with the chassis rather than having a separate body-on-frame.
A body of this type.
A shell that is the principal source of structural strength of an object; also, its design and construction.
examples: In selected cases where there is advanced (TASC) D aorto-iliac occlusive disease, treatment with a unibody stent-graft positioned at the aortic bifurcation is a safe and effective treatment.

senses: Exhibiting or practicing primitivism, the advocacy of primitive over refined forms
A large bronze coin minted during the Roman Empire.
ety: From Latin follis (“a bag”). Doublet of fals and fool.

senses: Involving multiple sectors
examples: As such, the triage process must take into account multisectoral (ie, water, food, sanitation, shelter, fuel, security) factors in making triage decisions.

senses: The act of vitalizing; enlivenment; vivification.
The lip, or edge of the aperture, of a spiral shell.
A painted or embroidered linen banner, usually depicting Buddhist themes, originating in Tibet; a prayer flag.
ety: Borrowed from Tibetan ཐང་ཀ (thang ka, literally “painting”).
examples: When the talks by Lama Thubten Yeshe on Buddhist and Christian meditation were published, the text included a reproduction of a Christian icon and a Tibetan thangka.

senses: Not contactable, not having a means by which contact can be made.
A tornado containing sharks.
A pungent green Japanese condiment made from the plant Eutrema japonicum (syn. Wasabia japonica).
An imitation of this condiment made from horseradish with green dye.
A fixation with healthy or righteous eating.
